pathetic

/puh-THET-ik/ — rhymes with 'athletic' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Pathetic is so weak or inadequate that it deserves pity or scorn.

The umbrella offered pathetic protection against the sideways hail.

Example

The school's 'security system' was pathetic: a rusty gate that no longer latched and a camera that had been broken for years. When bikes went missing from the rack, no one was surprised.

'Imperfect' security merely has some gaps; pathetic security is miserably inadequate, failing so completely it invites pity or scorn.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

pitiful: Pitiful means deserving pity for its weakness, and it leads with sympathy — a pitiful stray shivering in the rain invites kindness. Pathetic tips the same weakness into contempt: the failure is so complete that pity curdles into scorn. Call something pitiful and you feel sorry; call it pathetic and you may also sneer.

feeble: Feeble means weak and lacking force — a feeble grip, a feeble excuse. It describes the weakness itself without delivering a verdict. Pathetic is the verdict: a judgment that something failed so miserably it earns pity or scorn. A feeble attempt can still be forgiven; a pathetic one gets laughed at.

woeful: Woeful means deplorably bad — a woeful performance falls far below any acceptable standard. It overlaps with pathetic, but woeful measures how far short something falls, while pathetic adds the audience's reaction: pity, scorn, or laughter at how completely the thing failed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

admirable: deserving respect and approval

impressive: commanding attention through excellence

Where it sits · how badly it fails

mediocre → pathetic → abysmal

mediocre vs. pathetic: Mediocre is weaker than pathetic — mediocre work is merely average and forgettable, while pathetic work fails badly enough to invite scorn.

abysmal vs. pathetic: Abysmal is stronger than pathetic — pathetic means miserably inadequate, but abysmal means bottomlessly, catastrophically bad.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — path-: feeling, suffering (Greek)

suffix — -etic: relating to (Greek)

Put it together: Greek pathos means 'feeling' or 'suffering.' Pathetic originally meant 'stirring the feelings'; today it names things so inadequate that the feeling they stir is pity.

Use the root in a new word: sympathy: The whole class signed the sympathy card for their teacher.
